paras: The expulsion of the Russell Thomas family from Jones Station, Georgia, took place in the summer of 1920, when a white man, Grover Etheridge, forced the Black tenant farmer's two children to plow at pistol point and threatened Thomas with lynching. The family fled on foot to Macon, leaving behind their crop, livestock and goods, and the Chicago Defender reported them there penniless in early August.

Thomas, called by the Defender "a faithful old farmer," rented 38 acres and two mules at Jones Station from Mrs. Janie Etheridge, described as white, paying four bales of cotton a year for the land and $30 each for the mules. According to the report, his crop was doing well, his garden was planted, and the family owned two cows and a calf, more than a hundred chickens and 13 hogs.

On June 13, Grover Etheridge told Thomas that he had bought the property from his mother and that the tenants must do as he said. A few days later he came to the Thomas cabin leading two mules, while Mrs. Thomas, 14-year-old Alberta and eight-year-old Alvin were in the house. Armed with "a big stick and a pistol," he ordered the two children to take the mules into the field and plow until told to stop, and they obeyed.

The Defender's text, garbled in places, says Thomas was warned he would be lynched and that a blow was struck with the white man's "heavy club," though it is unclear whom it hit. That night the mother gathered the children and walked with them over a long road to Macon.

In Macon the family lived at 151 Franklin street with few clothes and household goods, and the report said they had not been allowed to return. A man named Young, of Beckwith street in Atlanta, was trying to recover their property; no report of an arrest or legal action against Etheridge was found.

The episode is known from a single front-page Chicago Defender story of August 7, 1920, datelined Macon, August 6, under the headline "Flees from Home to Escape Assault." The Defender framed it as racial oppression, writing that Thomas's "only crime was that his face was not white" and that he "could not demand his rights before local courts." It said he had been driven off because he "refused to let his children slave for a plantation owner"; no white-press report of the case was found.
